title: One hard case, five theories
subtitle: Adjudication in practice: interpretation, precedent and the judicial role
objectives: Distinguish textualist/originalist from purposive statutory interpretation, and the declaratory theory of precedent from judicial law-making
State how Hart's discretion-in-the-penumbra, Dworkin's Hercules and law-as-integrity, and CLS's indeterminacy thesis each predict a different account of the same hard case
Apply the theories from Lessons 1–14 to a single hard-case scenario and predict, accurately and fairly, what each school would say

leadingAuthorities.role: Permits courts, in limited circumstances, to consult Hansard to resolve genuine statutory ambiguity by reference to Parliament's purpose — a landmark for purposive interpretation
House of Lords abolishes the common law marital rape exemption; a central case study for the declaratory theory versus judicial law-making debate

leadingAuthorities.citation: Bell, Policy Arguments in Judicial Decisions (1983)
leadingAuthorities.role: Empirical and doctrinal study of how far, and how openly, judges reason using explicit policy arguments rather than rule-application alone

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This is the capstone lesson: it doesn't introduce a new theory, it asks you to run every theory you've studied through the same fact pattern and predict, honestly, what each one says — including the ones you find least persuasive. Where the profile shows knowledge ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can name Hercules and the rule of recognition — this lesson checks whether you can use them to answer a single hard question, correctly stated from each school's own point of view.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall across this module before. Every item below is scenario-first: you'll be asked what a named theory predicts about a specific case, not to define the theory in the abstract.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: If the school names from Lessons 4–13 (Hart, Dworkin, CLS, feminist theory) aren't automatic yet, revisit those lessons before this one — this capstone assumes you can retrieve each theory's core move without prompting, and spends its own time on applying it.

overview.hook: A park bylaw says: 'No vehicles in the park.' A warden stops a visitor riding an electric mobility scooter. Is a mobility scooter a 'vehicle'? H.L.A. Hart used exactly this kind of case to explain why rules have an 'open texture' — a core of settled meaning and a penumbra of genuine doubt. This lesson takes that single, deliberately narrow dispute and runs it through every major theory this module has covered: what would a textualist say, a purposivist, Hart, Dworkin's Hercules, a CLS scholar, a natural lawyer, a feminist or critical race theorist asking whose experience 'ordinary park user' was built around? None of them is simply right. The point of a capstone is to show you that the theories genuinely diverge on the same words — and to make you fluent enough in each to predict its answer before you're told it.
overview.lawStatedNotice: The park bylaw scenario used throughout this lesson is a standard teaching hypothetical (adapted from Hart's own example in his debate with Fuller, Lesson 6) rather than a real enactment; Pepper v Hart and R v R are real, settled leading authorities used to ground the interpretive and precedent doctrine the theories are then applied to.

parts.heading: Reading the words, or reading the purpose
parts.voice: argumentative — states each interpretive method's strongest case
body: Start with the bylaw itself: 'No vehicles in the park.' A textualist (and, in its strongest form, an originalist) approach reads the disputed word by its ordinary or established meaning at the time of enactment, resisting appeals to what the rule-maker 'really meant' beyond that text, on the ground that the enacted words — not unenacted intentions — are what was actually authorised and can be publicly known in advance. On a plain reading, a powered, wheeled means of transport is a vehicle; a mobility scooter is powered and wheeled; the scooter is caught, whatever hardship that causes the individual case.

A purposive approach reads the same words in light of the rule's evident objective — here, plausibly, protecting pedestrians from motorised traffic and preserving the park's quiet character — and asks whether applying the literal words to this case would serve or defeat that objective. On this method, a slow-moving mobility scooter, used by a visitor who needs it to be in the park at all, arguably falls outside what the bylaw was actually for, even though it falls within the bylaw's literal words.

English courts lean purposive, and Pepper v Hart [1993] AC 593 is the textbook illustration of how far that method can go: the House of Lords held that, where legislation is genuinely ambiguous or obscure, a court may consult Hansard — the record of parliamentary debate — to identify the mischief a statute was aimed at and Parliament's intention in enacting it, departing from a strict rule that had previously excluded such material. Textualists and originalists have long objected to this move on separation-of-powers grounds: debate is not law, a minister's stated intention is not what Parliament as a whole enacted, and using it risks judges finding the 'purpose' that produces the result they already favour. John Bell's Policy Arguments in Judicial Decisions (1983) documents just how openly English judges in fact reason from broader policy considerations once a case reaches genuine doubt — evidence, whatever you make of it, that purposive and policy-inflected reasoning is not a marginal judicial habit but a routine one.

components.definition: Textualism (and originalism, its stronger historical variant) interprets a legal text by its ordinary or established meaning, resisting appeals to unenacted intention; purposive interpretation reads the text in light of its evident objective, and will depart from a literal reading where the literal reading would defeat that objective.

interaction.prompt: In Pepper v Hart, what specifically did the House of Lords permit — and what is the strongest objection a textualist would raise?
options: It permitted courts to consult Hansard to resolve genuine statutory ambiguity by reference to Parliament's purpose; textualists object that debate and ministerial statements are not enacted law and risk being used to reach a predetermined result
It permitted courts to ignore the statutory text entirely whenever a judge personally disagreed with it
It abolished the distinction between primary and secondary legislation
interaction.trapExplanation: Pepper v Hart is a narrow, conditional permission (genuine ambiguity, clear ministerial statement directed at the point) — not a licence to override text, and it did not touch the primary/secondary legislation distinction at all. The genuine textualist objection is about legitimacy and manipulability, not about the rule being unlimited.

parts.heading: Declaring the law, or making it: R v R
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells R v R before naming the theoretical stakes
body: The classical declaratory theory of precedent, associated with Blackstone, holds that judges do not make law but discover and declare what the law has always been — even when a court overrules an earlier case, the theory says the earlier case was simply a mistaken statement of law that always existed, not a change to it. Legal realists, and most modern jurisprudence scholars, regard this as a useful fiction rather than an accurate description: a court that changes the law's practical effect for everyone going forward has, on any ordinary sense of the word, made new law.

R v R [1992] 1 AC 599 puts this dispute to the sharpest possible test. At common law, a long-standing exemption held that a husband could not be guilty of raping his wife, traced to Sir Matthew Hale's eighteenth-century statement that marriage constituted a wife's irrevocable consent to intercourse. The House of Lords held that the exemption no longer applied — that a wife's consent could be withdrawn, and 'unlawful' in the statutory definition of rape (then in the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 1976) did not exempt husbands.

The House of Lords chose declaratory language: it presented the exemption as a fiction that had never been a true rule of the common law at all, now simply corrected. Most academic commentary reads this very differently — as the House of Lords changing the law to match changed social and moral understanding of marriage and consent, using declaratory language to preserve the appearance of continuity and to avoid the rule-of-law concern (also relevant to the case's subsequent European Convention challenge) that retrospectively criminalising previously lawful conduct raises. Both readings agree on the outcome; they disagree entirely on what kind of thing the House of Lords did.

components.label: Declaratory theory vs judicial law-making, via R v R
points: Declaratory theory (Blackstone) — courts discover and declare pre-existing law; an overruled case was simply a mistaken statement, not a change
R v R's own framing — the House of Lords described the marital exemption as a fiction that had never truly been law, consistent with declaratory language

The realist/academic reading — the House of Lords in substance changed the law's practical effect, responding to changed social attitudes to marriage and consent, and used declaratory language to preserve legal continuity

The stakes — if R v R made new law, applying it to conduct that predated the decision raises a rule-of-law concern about retrospective criminalisation that the declaratory framing was partly designed to avoid

interaction.prompt: Put these steps in the order the R v R declaratory-theory debate proceeds.
items: The House of Lords holds the marital rape exemption no longer applies
The House of Lords frames this as removing a fiction that was never truly law, not as changing the law
Commentators point out this framing avoids a retrospective-criminalisation problem that a frank law-making account would raise
Scholars conclude the declaratory language is doing legitimating work, whatever the underlying reality of what the court did
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the shape of the academic debate: the outcome and its declaratory framing come first, and the realist reading is a step removed — an interpretation of why that framing was chosen.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order — start from what the House of Lords actually held and how it framed the holding, before moving to the academic critique of that framing.

parts.heading: Hart's penumbra, applied to the scooter
parts.voice: structural — walks a single theory through the fact pattern methodically
body: Return to the park bylaw. Hart's account (Lesson 5) holds that a rule like 'no vehicles in the park' has a core of settled meaning — a car, a motorbike, clearly a vehicle — and a penumbra of cases where the rule's application is genuinely unclear, because ordinary language and the rule-maker's foresight both run out. A mobility scooter sits, on Hart's account, in that penumbra: nothing in the rule of recognition or in the bylaw's settled core dictates an answer.

Hart's own view of what a judge should do here is precise and worth stating exactly, because it's often mis-stated. He does not say the judge may decide arbitrarily. He says the judge must exercise a genuine, first-order discretion — reasoning about what rule would be best, all things considered, informed by purposes, policy and values — because the existing legal materials, correctly understood, do not supply a uniquely correct answer. Crucially, for Hart this discretion is bounded and unusual, not routine: it operates only at the margins, in penumbral cases, and it does not threaten the determinacy of the vast core of settled law (a car is a vehicle; a mobility scooter's status is doubtful; a discarded shopping trolley is plainly not).

Applied here: Hart predicts the judge deciding the scooter case will — and should — openly acknowledge she is filling a gap the bylaw does not resolve, drawing on the bylaw's apparent purpose, considerations of disability access, and ordinary judicial common sense, and that a different judge, weighing those same considerations differently, could reasonably reach the opposite conclusion without either judge making a legal error.

components.definition: Hart's account of how judges decide genuinely doubtful cases: where a rule's core settled meaning does not resolve the dispute, the judge exercises a bounded, first-order discretion — reasoning to the best answer using purpose, policy and values — because the legal materials do not supply a uniquely correct answer at the margin, even though they do in the great bulk of ordinary, core cases.

interaction.prompt: On Hart's account, does judicial discretion in the penumbra mean a judge may decide a hard case arbitrarily, however she likes?
options: No — the discretion is genuine but bounded: the judge reasons to what she believes is the best rule, informed by purpose and policy, not an arbitrary choice
Yes — Hart's account treats penumbral decisions as entirely arbitrary and unreasoned
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. 'Discretion' in Hart's sense is a considered, reasoned judgment about the best answer at the margin — not a coin toss — even though he accepts that legal materials alone do not compel that answer.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again — Hart is explicit that this is a reasoned exercise of judgment, informed by purpose and policy, not an arbitrary or unreasoned choice. What he denies is that the legal materials alone dictate a single correct answer in these marginal cases.

parts.heading: Hercules and the indeterminacy thesis, applied to the same case
parts.voice: Socratic — sets Dworkin and CLS against each other on identical facts
body: Dworkin (Lessons 8–9) rejects Hart's account at exactly this point. His imagined ideal judge, Hercules, does not fill a gap by exercising discretion once legal materials run out — Dworkin denies the materials ever really run out. Hercules constructs the interpretation of the whole relevant body of law (the bylaw's text and evident purpose, related planning and access legislation, the general legal principle against arbitrary exclusion, disability-discrimination law's underlying commitments) that best fits the existing legal materials and shows them in their morally best light. On Dworkin's account there is, in principle, one right answer Hercules can reach through this constructive interpretation — even though ordinary judges, lacking Hercules's superhuman resources, may disagree about what it is. Applied here, Hercules is likely to conclude that a mobility scooter is not a 'vehicle' within the bylaw's justified meaning: that reading fits the text (scooters are marginal, not core, cases of 'vehicle') and best expresses a principle — equal access to public space — that the wider law can plausibly be read as already committed to.

CLS (Lesson 13) predicts something different again, and its prediction is not really about the scooter at all — it's about the dispute itself. A CLS scholar argues that the bylaw's text and purpose can each be read to support either conclusion (a scooter both obviously is, and obviously is not, the kind of thing a rule against 'vehicles' was written to catch), and that neither the textualist canon nor the purposive canon, applied with full formal competence, compels one answer over the other. The result, on this account, will track the individual judge's background commitment — an individualist commitment to rule-bound consistency and the certainty of clear categories, or an altruist/accommodationist commitment to context-sensitive fairness for the disabled visitor — dressed afterwards as a compelled reading of 'vehicle'. Notice what CLS and Dworkin agree and disagree about: both deny that the answer is a mechanical, gap-filling discretion in Hart's sense; they part company entirely on whether the 'best' answer Hercules reaches is a genuine, principled discovery, or simply Hercules's own political commitments in more sophisticated dress.

This is the single clearest three-way disagreement the module has produced: identical facts, identical text, three fully worked-out and mutually incompatible accounts of what a judge is doing when she decides the case.

components.label: Three predictions, same scooter
points: Hart — the bylaw's core meaning doesn't resolve this penumbral case; the judge exercises a bounded, reasoned discretion to fill the gap, and a different judge could reasonably decide the other way without legal error

Dworkin — Hercules constructs the interpretation that best fits and justifies the whole body of relevant law; there is, in principle, one right answer, even if ordinary judges disagree about what it is

CLS — the bylaw's text and purpose can support either answer with full doctrinal competence; the actual result tracks the judge's unstated individualist or altruist commitment, not a doctrinally compelled reading

interaction.prompt: A judge in the scooter case writes: 'The bylaw's language is unclear here, and having weighed the competing considerations, I conclude a mobility scooter is best treated as outside the rule's intended scope.' Which theory's predicted account does this judgment most closely match?
interaction.scenarioA: Hart's account of discretion in the penumbra — an open acknowledgment that the rule does not resolve the case, followed by a reasoned judgment about the best outcome.
interaction.scenarioB: Dworkin's Hercules — a claim that this is the single right answer uniquely required by the best constructive interpretation of the whole body of relevant law.
interaction.explanation: The judge's own language ('the language is unclear', 'having weighed the competing considerations') is Hart's discretion model stated almost verbatim — an acknowledged gap, filled by reasoned judgment. A Dworkinian judgment would instead present the answer as required by the best interpretation of the law as a whole, not as a discretionary choice between competing considerations.

parts.heading: Widening the lens: natural law, feminist theory and CRT on the same case
parts.voice: reflective — closes the module by returning to its full range of tools
body: The scooter case also tests theories this lesson hasn't yet applied to it. A natural lawyer in the Finnis tradition (Lesson 3) would ask whether excluding a disabled visitor from the park, on a literal reading, damages a basic good — sociability, or practical reasonableness itself — badly enough that the literal reading fails to be a fully reasonable specification of the rule, whatever its formal validity; a stricter natural law reading (closer to Aquinas, Lesson 2) might go further and ask whether applying the bylaw this way is unjust enough to fail to bind in conscience, even though it plainly remains valid law in the positivist sense. A Hartian positivist would resist this move at the level of validity (the bylaw is valid law regardless of how harsh a particular application is) while conceding that the harshness is a genuine reason for a court, exercising its penumbral discretion, to read the rule narrowly — moving the debate from validity to application, exactly where Hart insists it belongs.

A feminist or critical race theorist would ask a different, prior question: whose experience did 'the ordinary park user' — the implicit figure the bylaw's purpose was written around — assume? If the bylaw's drafters pictured an able-bodied adult on foot as the default, then a mobility-scooter user's needs were never part of the rule's contemplated 'core' at all — meaning the case looks penumbral only because the rule's core was built too narrowly in the first place. This is structurally the same move MacKinnon makes against the 'reasonable person' standard (Lesson 13) and the move CRT makes against facially neutral criteria that quietly encode one group's ordinary experience as the baseline (Lesson 14): the dispute isn't only about which category 'vehicle' captures, but about whose situation the category-builders had in view when they drew the line.

None of these five accounts — Hart, Dworkin, CLS, natural law, and the feminist/CRT question about whose experience counts as ordinary — is the 'correct' jurisprudence of the scooter case. Each is a fully worked-out, internally coherent way of describing what a court does, or should do, with the same six words. That plurality, stated precisely and defended fairly on every side, is what this module has been building towards from Lesson 1.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often try to rank the five accounts and declare one the 'right' jurisprudence of the case, or blend two incompatible accounts together (e.g. Hart's discretion plus Dworkin's one-right-answer thesis) without noticing they contradict each other.
components.whyItsWrong: The theories are not compatible variants of the same idea — Hart's discretion model and Dworkin's one-right-answer thesis are built to deny each other, and CLS denies both. This lesson tests whether you can state each account in a form its own author would recognise, not whether you can find a synthesis none of them would accept.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this argument that reflects the feminist/CRT-style question about whose experience a rule's 'core' meaning was built around, rather than a Hartian penumbra argument.
interaction.scenarioText: A commentator argues the scooter case looks 'penumbral' only because the bylaw's drafters pictured an able-bodied adult on foot as the default park user; on that reading, disabled visitors' needs were never part of the rule's settled core to begin with, so the case isn't really a hard case about an unclear penumbra at all.
tappableSpans: the scooter case looks 'penumbral' only because
the bylaw's drafters pictured an able-bodied adult on foot as the default park user
the case isn't really a hard case about an unclear penumbra at all
interaction.correctSpan: the bylaw's drafters pictured an able-bodied adult on foot as the default park user
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. This is the distinctive move: questioning whose experience was built into the rule's settled 'core' in the first place, rather than accepting the core as neutral and asking only how to resolve the penumbra around it.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the claim about whose experience shaped what counts as the rule's ordinary, settled application — that's the feminist/CRT-style challenge to the core itself, distinct from a Hartian argument about how to resolve genuine penumbral doubt.

testPool.prompt: State the difference between the declaratory theory of precedent and the judicial law-making view.
acceptableAnswers: declaratory theory says judges discover pre-existing law; law-making view says judges change the law
declaratory theory denies judges make new law, realists say they do
testPool.modelAnswer: The declaratory theory (Blackstone) holds that judges discover and declare law that already existed, even when overruling an earlier case; the judicial law-making view holds that a court which changes the law's practical effect going forward has, in substance, made new law, whatever language it uses to describe the decision.

testPool.prompt: In R v R, how did the House of Lords itself frame its abolition of the marital rape exemption?
options: As removing a fiction that had never truly been a rule of the common law, consistent with declaratory language
As an explicit, admitted change to the law, justified by changed social attitudes

testPool.prompt: Which of the following did Pepper v Hart NOT establish?
options: That Hansard may be consulted where legislation is genuinely ambiguous or obscure
That the material consulted must include a clear statement by the promoter of the legislation directed to the point in question
That courts may override the text of a statute whenever a judge finds Hansard more persuasive than the words enacted
That the rule marks a departure from an earlier, stricter exclusionary approach to using parliamentary material
testPool.trapExplanation: Pepper v Hart is a narrow, conditional exception, not a general licence to prefer Hansard over the enacted text — a court still starts from, and remains bound by, the statutory words; Hansard resolves genuine ambiguity, it does not license overriding clear text.

testPool.prompt: Order these steps in Hart's account of deciding the scooter case.
items: Identify the bylaw's core settled meaning (a car is plainly a vehicle)
Recognise the scooter sits in the penumbra, where the rule's application is genuinely unclear
Exercise a bounded, reasoned discretion, informed by the bylaw's purpose and relevant policy, to reach the best answer
Accept that a different judge, weighing the same considerations differently, could reasonably reach the opposite conclusion without legal error

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, summarising Dworkin's account of Hercules, highlight the sentence that most precisely states his 'one right answer' claim.
testPool.passage: Hercules constructs the interpretation of the whole relevant body of law that best fits the existing legal materials and shows them in their morally best light. On Dworkin's account there is, in principle, one right answer Hercules can reach through this constructive interpretation — even though ordinary judges, lacking Hercules's resources, may disagree about what it is.
testPool.ratioSentence: On Dworkin's account there is, in principle, one right answer Hercules can reach through this constructive interpretation — even though ordinary judges, lacking Hercules's resources, may disagree about what it is.

testPool.prompt: A CLS scholar argues both the textualist and purposive readings of 'no vehicles in the park' can be defended with equal formal competence. Which conclusion follows most directly from that observation, on CLS's own account?
options: The eventual result tracks the judge's unstated background commitment (rule-bound consistency versus context-sensitive accommodation), not a doctrinally compelled reading
The bylaw must therefore be struck down as void for uncertainty
Textualism is thereby proven false and purposive interpretation is thereby proven correct

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that Hart's and Dworkin's accounts of the scooter case are compatible — that is, that both can be correct at once?
sliderLabels: Not confident — the accounts are built to deny each other
Confident — the two accounts are compatible
testPool.correctPosition: Not confident — the accounts are built to deny each other
testPool.explanation: Not confident is correct. Hart holds that legal materials run out in penumbral cases, requiring discretion; Dworkin denies this, holding that constructive interpretation of the whole legal and moral landscape yields one right answer even in hard cases. They cannot both be a correct description of the same case.

testPool.prompt: Which judicial statement reflects a natural-law-style objection (Lessons 2–3) to a literal reading of the bylaw, rather than a Hartian penumbra argument?
testPool.scenarioA: 'The bylaw's language does not clearly resolve this case; weighing the relevant considerations, I find a scooter falls outside its intended scope.'
testPool.scenarioB: 'Excluding a disabled visitor who depends on this scooter to be in the park at all would be so damaging to the basic good of participation in public life that a literal reading fails to be a reasonable specification of the rule, whatever its formal validity.'
testPool.explanation: B invokes damage to a basic good (participation, sociability) and practical reasonableness as a constraint on what counts as a reasonable application of valid law — a natural-law-style move. A is Hart's discretion model: an acknowledged gap, resolved by reasoned judgment, with no claim about basic goods or the limits of what can count as reasonable law.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this argument that reflects Bell's point (Policy Arguments in Judicial Decisions) about how openly English judges reason from policy, rather than a strict textualist argument.
testPool.scenarioText: In her judgment, the judge writes that a literal reading of 'vehicle' would technically catch the scooter, but that she is persuaded a purposive reading, informed by the wider policy of promoting disabled access to public spaces, is the better approach, and she says so in those terms rather than presenting the result as compelled by the bare words.
tappableSpans: a literal reading of 'vehicle' would technically catch the scooter
informed by the wider policy of promoting disabled access to public spaces
she says so in those terms rather than presenting the result as compelled by the bare words
testPool.correctSpan: she says so in those terms rather than presenting the result as compelled by the bare words
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right. Bell's empirical point is precisely that judges often openly acknowledge reasoning from policy rather than concealing it behind a claim of textual compulsion — this is that openness in action.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact about the judge's candour, not the substance of her reasoning. Bell's point is about the visibility of policy reasoning in judgments, which is captured by her saying so openly rather than dressing the result as textually compelled.

testPool.prompt: A second hard case: a bylaw bans 'dogs off the lead' in a park; a visitor carries a small, calm dog in a closed bag rather than walking it on a lead. Applying Hart's account, what should the deciding judge do?
options: Openly acknowledge that 'off the lead' does not clearly resolve a dog carried in a bag, and exercise a bounded, reasoned discretion — informed by the bylaw's evident safety purpose — to reach the best available answer
Refuse to decide the case on the ground that all penumbral cases are non-justiciable
Apply the bylaw literally regardless of purpose, since Hart's account requires strict textualism in every case
testPool.explanation: This is a direct transfer of Hart's model: the case sits in the rule's penumbra, and Hart's account calls for acknowledged, reasoned discretion informed by purpose — not refusal to decide, and not mechanical textualism, which is not Hart's position at all.

testPool.prompt: Using CLS's indeterminacy thesis, analyse the 'dogs off the lead' bag scenario from the previous item, explaining why doctrine alone cannot dictate the answer and what will actually determine the outcome on CLS's account.
factsToOrder: The bylaw's text specifies 'off the lead', not 'not under physical control'
A textualist reading could treat a bagged dog as literally 'off the lead' and so caught
A purposive reading, focused on public safety, could treat a controlled, bagged dog as outside the rule's concern
Both readings are available using the accepted materials with equal formal competence

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether legal doctrine alone determines whether a dog carried in a closed bag is 'off the lead' within the bylaw.
modelAnswer.rule: CLS's indeterminacy thesis: where accepted interpretive methods (textualist and purposive) can each be applied with equal formal competence to support opposite conclusions, doctrine does not compel a single result — an unstated background value choice does.
modelAnswer.application: A textualist reading of 'off the lead' literally catches the bagged dog; a purposive reading focused on public safety plausibly excludes it, since the dog is controlled. Nothing in the accepted materials of legal reasoning forces a court to prefer one canon over the other here — the eventual choice will reflect the judge's own weighting of certainty/rule-bound consistency against context-sensitive accommodation.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Doctrine alone cannot dictate the answer; on CLS's account, the actual outcome is explained by which background value the judge foregrounds, not by a legally compelled reading of 'off the lead'.

testPool.prompt: Applying Dworkin's Hercules to the 'dogs off the lead' bag scenario, what method should the judge use to decide it?
options: Construct the interpretation of the whole relevant body of law — the bylaw's text and purpose, related animal-control and public-safety principles — that best fits those materials and shows them in their morally best light, and treat the resulting answer as the one right answer
Toss a coin, since Dworkin holds that hard cases are genuinely undecidable
Apply whichever canon of interpretation produces the harsher penalty, as Dworkin requires deterrence to be prioritised
testPool.explanation: This restates Hercules's method precisely: constructive interpretation aimed at the best fit and justification across the relevant legal materials, yielding — on Dworkin's account — a single right answer, not an arbitrary or formulaic one.

testPool.prompt: R v R involved the phrase 'unlawful sexual intercourse' in the then-applicable statutory definition of rape. Which interpretive method did the House of Lords effectively use to hold that 'unlawful' did not exempt husbands?
options: A purposive reading, informed by evolving understanding of marriage and consent, departing from Hale's eighteenth-century assumption despite the word 'unlawful' having previously been read as importing that exemption
A strict textualist reading of the word 'unlawful' by its plain eighteenth-century dictionary meaning
No interpretation of the statute was involved; the decision rested entirely on European Convention grounds

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is blending two incompatible theories together — for example, describing Hart's bounded discretion in Dworkinian 'one right answer' language, or vice versa. Each theory is tested here for its own internal logic applied to the same facts; the test items reward precision about which account you're using, not a synthesis none of the original authors would recognise.
